Write a short story or a fairy tale in the Präteritum.
It's an evening in November. Kasia and Piotr are at a concert, and Mara is looking after Kuba and Ola. The twins want a story before bed. Bruno is asleep between the beds.
Mara, will you tell us a fairy tale? But not Little Red Riding Hood. We already know that one.
Hm. Shall I tell you a Romanian fairy tale? About Făt-Frumos (the Romanian Prince Charming)?
No, tell us a fairy tale about you! A true one!
About me? All right, then. Once upon a time there was a young woman. She lived in a town with roofs that had eyes.
A little. One day she packed her bags and went to a big, strange city. She didn't know anybody there. She was afraid.
And then? Did a witch come?
No. She rang at a door and an old man opened it. He had once been the king of the trams. And he had a small, long dragon.
That's Fritz! Fritz isn't a dragon!
In the fairy tale he is. He guarded the king's treasure: a sausage.
And what happened to the young woman then?
She found friends. A baker who did magic at four in the morning. An old pianist in a tower. And two children who saved a dog called Bruno. And if they haven't died…
…they're still alive today. On Kastanienallee! Good night, Mara.
“es war einmal” = once upon a time
Listen to the vowel change: kommen → kam, sehen → sah, bleiben → blieb, schreiben → schrieb.
German has two past tenses which mean practically the same thing. The difference is one of STYLE:
in writing: books, fairy tales, news, reports
in speech: conversations, messages, personal emails
The exceptions you already know: sein, haben and the modal verbs are used in the Präteritum in speech too (war, hatte, konnte, musste).
ich and er / sie have the same form: “ich wohnte”, “sie wohnte”. Separable verbs split here too: “Sie packte den Koffer ein.” “Er rief sie an.”
Irregular verbs change their vowel and do NOT take -te. With ich and er / sie they have no ending at all:
“Mixed” verbs (changed vowel + -te): denken → dachte, wissen → wusste, bringen → brachte, kennen → kannte, nennen → nannte.
The best way to learn them: by reading stories. The stories in chapters 22–32 are full of them: kam, ging, sah, stand, saß…

Wie meine Schwester nach Berlin kam

From Andrei Ionescu's brown notebook, “The stories of Kastanienallee”, page 41. Ludwig said I should also write a story about our family. Here it is. I'm writing it in the Präteritum, because Mara says that's how stories are written. The mistakes are my own.

Once upon a time there was a young nurse in Sibiu. Her name was Mara and she was my sister. She worked in a hospital where there were too few staff and too little money. She often worked sixty hours a week and still didn't earn enough to pay for a flat of her own. In the evenings she sat in her old childhood bedroom and studied German, from books she had bought at the flea market. I didn't understand why. I was eighteen and thought German was a language for old teachers.

One day a letter came from Berlin. A hospital was looking for nurses. Mara read the letter three times, then put it on the kitchen table and said nothing. Mum saw the letter and cried. Dad saw the letter and went to his bees. I saw the letter and asked: “Can I have your room?”

In October we drove her to the airport. She had two suitcases and a bag with three jars of honey, which Dad had secretly packed for her. At the airport she hugged Mum for a long time. Then she hugged Dad, who said nothing but kept his hand on her shoulder for a long time. Then she hugged me and whispered: “Look after Mum.” I promised. Then she went through the door and disappeared. On the way back, in the car, nobody spoke. At home I went into her room. I didn't want it any more.

In Berlin, Mara found a small flat on the third floor of an old building. The landlord was a former tram driver with a dachshund. He gave her the keys on the first evening and said “Welcome”. Mara told us later on the phone that she couldn't sleep the first night. She stood at the window, looked at a chestnut tree in the courtyard and thought: what am I doing here? I don't know anybody. I don't understand half of what I hear. Tomorrow my first shift starts.

The first weeks were hard. Mara called every evening, and Mum held the phone so that we could all see her face. She always smiled, but we could see her eyes were tired. She told us about patients who spoke Berlin dialect and whom she didn't understand, about a tram called the M1, about an old man who played the guitar every evening, very quietly and very out of tune. Once, in November, she cried on the phone. She had got lost in the city and had walked from Museum Island to Kreuzberg without realising. Mum wanted to buy a plane ticket straight away. Dad took the phone out of her hand and said just one sentence: “Mara, bees always find their way home too. Even when they get lost.” The next evening, Mara was laughing again. In Kreuzberg she had met a doctor from her hospital, who had invited her for tea.

But then something happened that always happens in fairy tales. She found friends. First a dog that waited outside her door. Then a baker who gave her warm bread rolls after the night shift. Then a colleague who invited her for coffee and showed her how you pay in Germany: separately. Then an old pianist on the fourth floor, who played every evening at nine. And the old tram driver, who taught her German while she explained his phone to him.

I came to Berlin for the first time at Easter. Actually I only wanted to visit my sister. But on the second day I was standing in a bakery at four in the morning, shaping pretzels that looked like snakes. The baker laughed at my pretzels. I fell in love with her laugh. Everyone on Kastanienallee knows the rest of the story, so I won't write it here. Lena reads this notebook too.

Now I'm in Berlin myself, for a semester at the Technical University. I live at Mara's, on the sofa that by now almost bears my name, and I'm on Kastanienallee every day. At four in the morning in the bakery, in the evening at Ludwig's under the yellow lamp, on Sundays at the Nowaks', where Bruno greets me every time as if I'd been away for three years. Sometimes in the evening I sit in the courtyard under the chestnut tree and look up at the windows: the yellow light on the first floor, the blue light of Kuba's bedside lamp on the second, Mara's window on the third, where she's still studying for her specialisation, and right at the top, on the fourth, the open window that music comes from at nine o'clock. And then I think that this house has eyes too, like those houses in Sibiu. Only these eyes don't watch. They care.

Today it's November, and Mara has been in Berlin for more than two years. She has a permanent contract, a B1 exam with “very good” in speaking and a goddaughter who will be born in December. Every Tuesday she teaches Romanian at the neighbourhood centre, to seven students, among them Lena, who after three months can already say “Andrei e un dezastru” (Andrei is a disaster), with a perfect accent. Mum calls every Sunday and asks when Mara is coming back. Mara always says: “Soon, Mum.” And Mum always says: “I know that's not true.” Then they both laugh.

Ludwig read this story yesterday. He took off his glasses, wiped them for a long time and said: “Well written, lad. Just one mistake. A sentence is missing at the end.” I asked him which one. He took my pen and wrote in his big, shaky handwriting under my story:

“And if they haven't died, they're still alive today. In an old house with a chestnut tree in the courtyard, a yellow lamp on the first floor and a piano under the roof. And they're not alone. Not one of them.”

Read the beginning of a famous fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm, simplified. Listen twice. At the end there are 4 questions.
Once upon a time there was an old donkey. He had worked for a farmer for many years, but now he was too old and too weak.
The farmer didn't want him any more. So the donkey ran away. He wanted to go to Bremen and become a musician there.
On the way he met an old dog, an old cat and an old rooster. Nobody wanted them any more.
The donkey said: “Come with me to Bremen! We'll find something better than death anywhere.”
So the four of them went on together. They never arrived in Bremen. But they found a house in the forest and lived there happily together.
